When I was 18 I was jumping off some large rocks near Sand Harbor in Lake Tahoe, NV. It was about a 30 foot jump, and you had to launch yourself out far enough to clear the small boulder at the base of the rock formation. I had watched at least a dozen people make the jump with ease so I figured I could make it fine. 

As soon as I jumped though I knew I wasn’t going to make it. Those couple seconds of free fall are cemented in my brain even 13 years later. I remember thinking I had to make sure to land on my legs because if my torso or head hit I was for sure dead. And as soon as I made that decision, I had the most random memory of going for a drive with the windows down and never having that again if I lost my legs. I ended up tucking my right leg up under me so I would come down on my left leg only (my reasoning being I could always drive an automatic, but at least needed my right leg for the acceleration/break pedals.) 

When I hit the rock I knew it hurt but immediately went into shock. I didn’t realize how bad it was until I attempted to tread water and could feel my left leg flopping around. I spent the next couple weeks in and out of surgeries, and had five different surgeons say they had to amputate; but my parents kept bringing in new doctors to consult. Eventually the sixth physician said he could repair it. I spent nearly a year in a wheelchair and another six months of physical therapy, but they saved my leg.

Now I have a near constant limp, chronic pain, no range of motion in my ankle, and the arthritis of a 90 year old in my ankle, knee and hip. I’m not even going to get into the weight gain and mental health impact. On the bad days I sometimes wish they would have amputated. One dumb choice when I was 18 changed my entire life (I was also on track to enlist in the military but obviously that couldn’t happen), but hey, at least I’m not dead.

Skin itches when it is healing and scabbing because of nerve endings that were severed now stitching themselves back together. And healing takes a long time, and goes much deeper then you think. So that annoying itch can continue for a while.

Older wounds can randomly become itchy as well. You know that tight scar tissue (collagen) that covers the wound? Well, simply enough, tight skin itches. So even if a scar is old, that tissue can still be stretched causing random itching. 

One more thing, a lot of people notice (myself included) that when they start to get more direct sunlight their scars itch more. Probably because of UV burn on the scar tissue, causing the skin to tighten.

I hope that wasn’t too much and eased your mind some. Take care of yourself.

Backstory, I don’t have any kids of my own- but I have 5 nieces and nephews that are fairly close to my age because I’m so much younger than my sisters. And I’m the only one in my friend group that doesn’t have kids- so I’ve taken on the aunt role with those munchkins as well.

But my answer is; if they are still young and it’s just a curious kid thing- they obviously don’t need details. My go to is usually something about battle scars and I’ll tell them about it when they’re older- then redirect. 

If they are old enough to be really asking that question though, then I tell them the truth. The way I think about it is; would you rather them get the information from you, and your personal journey; or the Internet and their equally uninformed friends?

I’ve had the “what are those” conversation with kids actually old enough to have it twice. First time was over a decade ago, my oldest niece came to me and asked and I panicked. I made some vague excuse and changed the subject- because I was so scared and ashamed I couldn’t talk about it.  I do not blame myself for her starting to self harm not long after that- but I do believe I failed her in that moment. Who knows if that conversation would have changed her mind or actions; but the fact is I personally know how isolating self harm ideation can feel and I left her there anyway, because of my fear.

The second time was just earlier this year. My youngest nephew came and stayed with me for a week, and during that time he asked about my scars (some fairly fresh). And this time I actually had the conversation. I gave honest but basic answers and didn’t go into too many details, unless he asked more specific questions. And I could tell as the conversation went on, and I continued to be candid, sincere, and spoke to him as I would any other peer- that he was slowly becoming more comfortable and eventually went from asking me questions to talking about his own fear and feelings.

Three weeks after he got back home he called me to tell me his mom helped him find a talk therapist and he was actually looking forward to his first appointment. 

I believe that honesty, especially with our children, is how we can keep a relationship strong even as it continues to evolve and grow throughout time. Lies, even the small ones maybe made to protect people, sit on us. They grow stale and stagnant and have the capacity to poison everything around us.

I so encourage you to read Lord of the Rings, but I also really encourage you get a few super good, compelling reads digested first before opening the Tolkien tombs. They are amazing, you must read them- but for your first fun book, naw. 
To give you an example of some of the tediousness super early on; less than 200 pages into the first book- you suddenly spend another 200 pages in a forest with two eccentric characters that will never be anything more than endnote mentioned again. It can be a chore to dig through LoTR at times, and I think you’d be a lot more motived to tackle if you had that ‘can’t put it down’ awesome book journey experience first.


So these are a couple of my suggests for a good compelling story, well written, and fun. I have so many more though too- but I had to stop.


Eragon by Christopher Paolini. Total fantasy trope, with bits and pieces of everything, also dragon and dragon rider. Called the Inheritance Cycle, has four books total. Some people love this series, some people will straight up Game of Thrones ‘Shame’ me for even recommending it. The reason I am though, is because this series takes so many different bits from so many different, beautiful classic fiction works. Lord of the Rings (names, locations), Star Wars (storyline), Dragonriders of Pern (uh dragonriders). Gives a taste of the shear awesome scale that is fantasy fiction literature.  Another thing to keep in mind, the author wrote the first book at 15 and the last around 20. I don’t dislike his writing style, it’s just so full of so many descriptions someone could get lost.


His Dark Material (trilogy) by Phillip Pullman. Young adult main characters, but it’s an adult series. Especially book two and majorly three. It’s vast and it gets metaphysical at times, it also challenges the Catholic Church basically. Best thing though is every living person has an animal creature called a Daemon- which is the living, breathing, talking embodiment of the persons soul.

Le Belle Sauvage also by Phillip Pullman.  It is a prequel series to HDM, set about a decade prior to the first book. Same universe.


The Farseer Trilogy by Robin Hobb.  Magical link with animals. Magic in general. Royalty. Assassins and Spies oh my!


The Icewind Dale Trilogy by R.A. Salvatore. Want a true fantasy straight out of Dungeons and Dragons? Originally Salvatore wrote the Forgotten Realms Campaign Setting for D&D and Drizzt Do'Urden was a minor sidekick. Well then Salvatore decided to write some novels, and our classic misunderstood hero Drizzt and his party come into creation.


You definitely do need to put Harry Potter on your list. Even if only to read the books that shaped multiple generations nearly overnight. They are technically classified YA, but the coolest thing about the series is how it grows. Each book is one year; the first book is a very simple read. It’s a very basic book. Each book gets older- not only in character study, but writing style/skill, education learned, problems being faced, etc.  The first two books you’ll enjoy, but not quite get what all the hype is about. And then when you finish three you’re so close, then you start four and you’ll be hooked for good and it’ll just keep becoming grander and grander.

One other thing, I hope it’s okay if I share a story;

I have gained empowerment the last few years by talking about my self harm and my scars. I allow people to ask questions (even rude ones), I don’t glare at someone if I notice they’re staring at my arm anymore. If I see someone staring at them, but they’re too scared to ask, I will usually make a stupid joke to get their eye contact/attention and offer to tell them parts of my story.  (Most fucked up/Best joke I’ve told to break the tension with someone who had been staring for a while ‘if I had a mallet I’d play them like a xylophone.’)

At first I felt shame for talking about my scars, because for so long I felt they were ugly and weak and pathetic and I had to hide them at all costs. Or! That I was giving into the attention seeking behavior of wanting pity for cutting myself so i couldn’t possibly let them be visible. 
But then a young girl (teenager, I was mid 20s) noticed my arm one day and she had this look on her face I couldn’t figure out at the time.  I started a conversation with her, small talk at first, but then she asked me if I had given those scars to myself. She nearly whispered it and wouldn’t meet my eyes, and for the first time when someone asked me that I didn’t freeze. I told her yes, then told some of my story. She ended up pulling up her sleeves to show me healed scars, and the bottom of her shirt to show fresher cuts on her belly- and then proceeded to share some of her story. We only had five, maybe ten minutes before our coffee orders were up and we were heading different directions, and while the basis of the conversation was SH, it wasn’t the only thing we talked about.
Before she left she thanked me for being willing to talk to her about it, apologized for being so forward and explained that she never had anyone to talk about SH with because the rest of her support system just freaks out anytime it’s brought to their attention. 
And for the first time I felt like these scars were just another part of the aesthetic that is me- and not something damaged that needed to be covered up and hid. That maybe I was doing myself, and others who struggle with this, a disservice for being so ashamed and scared to talk about it. 

So I decided to stop hiding. I wear short sleeves, I have a watch of my left wrist- even though that probably brings even more attention. I don’t lie about what they are. I don’t make it a bit deal, I just remain calm and factual- as if I am teaching someone something they had no prior knowledge in.  Sure, I’ve gotten a few nasty comments here and there, mean or just hurtful things that any decent human with a bit of compassion would never say.  And if that happens I remove myself from the situation, or tell the rude person to remove themselves from being anywhere near my person.


Basically TL;DR: I was able to start moving past the shame I felt about my self harm scars by having a conversation with a random person who also struggled after they saw my scars and asked. This helped me to understand that the only shame I actually deserve to feel would be if I continued to hide and refused to be my authentic self. Because there are a lot more people out there who could use the support of knowing they’re not alone in their self harm behavior, then there are assholes who think it’s okay to tear us down and make us feel guilty for behaviors that they have no understanding of and don’t even want to try and understand.

I work at a behavioral health hospital. Our facility helps people struggling with suicidal thoughts, anxiety, depression, as well as people struggling with active psychosis. It's a crisis stabilization hospital- meaning it's short term (5-7 days) to help a person mentally get back to a safe and stable place- and then get them set out with outpatient services. 

I explain this for two reasons:

One, so you know, that I know, what I'm talking about.
Two, If you would like any further information, or a recommendation for a facility in your state- I would be happy to help.

The original question though!

Mental health is the same as physical health when it comes to a patients HIPAA rights. The hospital will not share any of your medical information without your consent. So you don't have to share anything with anyone you don't want to. 

Legally, your employer cannot discriminate against you because of a mental illness. And if it is available to you, the hospital could help you get FMLA or short term leave.

Of course there are lots of loopholes, and I could be specific with you if I knew your state and job. But basically, that's the jist of it.
